Fortunately, eBPF tracing has emerged as a powerful tool for optimizing network performance. **Overall, eBPF tracing provides a powerful and versatile tool for optimizing network performance.**. When done correctly, eBPF tracing can provide developers with critical insights into what is happening in their systems, which can lead to improved performance, better debugging, and more. **4) Utilize Debugging Tools:**Debugging tools such as GDB or LLDB can be extremely helpful when troubleshooting an issue related to an eBPF trace, as they allow you to view information on threads running on an application in real-time. eBPF tracing is emerging as a potent tool that can be used to optimize performance, identify performance issues, and generally improve user experience. Netflix also leveraged eBPF tracing to enhance its performance monitoring capabilities. The use of eBPF tracing in cloud and high-performance computing has opened up several new possibilities for system administrators, developers, and users. For example, administrators can use eBPF tracing to identify bottlenecks within their cloud infrastructure, allowing them to make adjustments to increase efficiency and performance. As the world transitions towards technological advancements at an unprecedented pace, it's no surprise that the future of eBPF tracing and Linux performance monitoring is set to transform the software development industry. The increased flexibility and versatility of eBPF tracing allows developers to analyze system performance at a micro-level, aiding in creating more efficient and optimized programs. Overall, the end of eBPF tracing and Linux performance monitoring is set to be a game-changer, improving system performance and positively impacting the user experience. Adopting an eBPF tracing approach is a great way to optimize an application's performance, improve stability, and better understand its inner workings.

results.title: Debugging with eBPF Part 2: Tracing full body HTTP request/responses | Pixie Labs Blog
results.content: # Debugging with eBPF Part 2: Tracing full body HTTP request/responses. In this second post, we will look at how to use eBPF to capture HTTP 1.X traffic. Many applications accomplish this by utilizing middleware to add tracing or logging to HTTP requests in the application. In this post, we will take a look at an alternative approach that utilizes eBPF to capture HTTP data without having to manually add instrumentation. Since applications typically sit on top of the Kernel system API, if we capture the Kernel interface we should be able to capture all the ingress and egress data and reconstruct the HTTP requests. Alternatively, we can use uprobes to carefully instrument underlying HTTP libraries (eg. net/http in Go) to capture HTTP requests directly. This post will explore tracing HTTP requests using both kprobes and uprobes and compare the tradeoffs for each. Before we start writing any BPF code, let’s try to understand how HTTP requests are handled by the system. The first step is to understand what Linux kernel APIs are used to send and receive data for a simple HTTP request. Tracing these system calls should allow us to capture all of the data the server is sending out in response to a request. While the focus of this example is on tracing the HTTP response, it is also possible to trace the data sent in the HTTP request by adding a probe to the `read` syscall. We write out this data to a perf buffer so the userspace tracing program can read it. Once the data is captured, we can read it to our Go userspace program and parse the HTTP response using the `net/http` library. An alternative approach is to use uprobes to capture the data before it gets sent to the kernel where we can read the data before it has been serialized. 9 0x0000000000632c61 in net/http.(*response).finishRequest at /opt/golang/src/net/http/server.go:1588. We captured HTTP requests of various durations by increasing the `iterations` parameter of the `computeE` function on our app.go http server. Tracing HTTP requests using eBPF is possible using both kprobes and uprobes; however, the kprobe approach is more scalable as it is agnostic to the target language.

results.content: * To enable a particular event, simply echo it to /sys/kernel/tracing/set_event. root@rog /s/k/tracing# cd events/syscalls/sys_enter_getpeername/ root@rog /s/k/t/e/s/sys_enter_getpeername# ls enable filter format hist id trigger root@rog /s/k/t/e/s/sys_enter_getpeername# echo 1 > enable * kprobes let you dynamically change the **Linux kernel’s assembly code at runtime** (like, insert extra assembly instructions) to trace when a given instruction is called. * Add probe points via /sys/kernel/debug/tracing/uprobe_events, and enable it via /`sys/kernel/debug/tracing/events/uprobes/<EVENT>/enable` * However unlike kprobe-event tracer, the uprobe event interface expects the user to calculate the offset of the probepoint in the object. **Ways to extract data :** Credits: Julia Evans * tracefs is a pseudo file system that provides an interface to the kernel's trace events * tracefs is mounted at /sys/kernel/tracing * tracefs is used by ftrace, perf, and eBPF to access trace events * tracefs can be mount using `mount -t tracefs nodev /sys/kernel/tracing`**Note** : For backward compatibility, when mounting the debugfs file system, the tracefs file system will be automatically mounted at: `/sys/kernel/debug/tracing` * Ftrace is a tracing tool that is built into the Linux kernel. results.title: eBPF-Based Auto-Instrumentation Outperforms Manual Instrumentation | Odigos Blog
results.content: Our performance tests, which we’ll go into below, show that eBPF-based automatic instrumentation is over 20x faster than manually instrumenting code. As a result, you can have the best of both worlds: automated distributed tracing with minimal performance overhead. ## **The performance impact of generating distributed traces**. When using eBPF to generate distributed traces, we are separating the recording of the data from the processing of the data. Odigos solves this problem by providing a way to automate distributed tracing that actually improves performance. This is because we use eBPF-based automatic instrumentation to reduce the overhead of generating distributed tracing data. **As a result, you can now have the best of both worlds: automated distributed tracing without any performance overhead**. eBPF-based automatic instrumentation is a game-changer, enabling us to generate distributed traces **without code changes** or **performance impact**. The easiest way to try eBPF-based distributed tracing today is to use our open-source project, Odigos.
